title: Accessible lifetime retirement income through transparent, resilient risk pooling

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a replicable retirement-income arrangement that combines efficient longevity pooling, broad access, low total cost and understandable, enforceable rules for sharing financial risks. Participants pool resources so that those who live longer can continue receiving payments after they would otherwise have exhausted their individual savings. Existing annuities and collective arrangements already provide forms of this protection; the proposed advance is demonstrating the full combination at substantial scale, including for people with small retirement balances.

Pooling individual longevity risk means sharing uncertainty about which participants will live unusually long. It does not eliminate aggregate longevity risk, such as an entire population living longer than expected, or investment and funding risks. The design would make these remaining exposures explicit and specify how contributions, benefits or other financial commitments change when available resources diverge from expectations. A payment continuing for life and a payment remaining adequate throughout life are separate outcomes.

Design synthesis: this is a combined actuarial and institutional goal. Benefit formulas and financial models would need to work together with governance, regulation, administration and communication so that participants can understand their rights and the circumstances under which payments may change. The supplied evidence establishes a relevant design problem and existing technical foundations, but does not establish whether the complete proposed capability remains undemonstrated in 2026.

significance.text: If demonstrated with substantially broader access and radically lower total cost, the arrangement could extend protection against outliving savings to retirees poorly served by existing products or pension plans. Its revolutionary significance would depend on the magnitude and reach of that improvement over operating alternatives. Longevity pooling itself is already established, and neither radical cost reductions nor broad participation follows automatically from using a pool.

Transparent loss allocation would make a consequential feature of collective retirement provision easier to assess: whose benefits or financial obligations change when experience disappoints. The OECD describes how collective ownership can smooth investment outcomes across cohorts, while also making the distribution of risk difficult to see. It also explains that individually defined ownership rights can make risk sharing more transparent. The opportunity is therefore to demonstrate understandable rights and resilient pooling together, rather than assume opacity is unavoidable in every collective arrangement.

Conditional downstream synthesis: a successful, replicable design could make lifetime-income options easier to offer through more retirement systems and help participants compare the protection purchased with their savings. Those possibilities would depend on local institutions, participant uptake and implementation costs. The supplied material contains no quantitative impact estimate or historical breakthrough benchmark against which to establish the scale of such effects.

The protection remains bounded by resources. A scheme can preserve financial balance by adjusting benefits to the assets available, but those adjustments may reduce income below participants’ needs. Pooling does not establish adequate lifetime benefits under every possible demographic and market outcome; any promised protection against shortfalls must identify the resources and party supporting that promise.

missing_breakthrough.text: The proposed breakthrough is demonstrating broad access, low total cost, transparent loss allocation and resilient lifetime payments together in a design that can be replicated across populations. These goals can conflict: smoothing benefits may redistribute risks across cohorts, while a financially sustainable adjustment can reduce payment adequacy. The OECD’s 2022 discussion establishes relevant challenges and existing solutions, but cannot establish that this combined target remains unsolved as of 2026-11-01.

A central actuarial barrier is specifying how the scheme measures financial imbalance and allocates the resulting mismatch. The design must distinguish uncertainty that can be shared among individuals from adverse experience affecting the pool as a whole. It must also make the consequences of ownership and benefit-adjustment rules visible across cohorts. Smoothing payments changes when and among whom financial consequences are borne; it does not remove the underlying exposure.

Engineering synthesis: unresolved implementation work includes keeping administration and governance affordable for small balances, communicating conditional benefits accurately, and specifying entry and exit rules that make transfers between participants intelligible. Replication would require identifying which results depend on population characteristics, regulatory permissions or support from employers and providers. These are proposed requirements for the combined capability, rather than evidence that every existing arrangement fails them.

current_state.text: The OECD chapter published in OECD Pensions Outlook 2022 on 1 December 2022 documents lifetime annuities and collective retirement-income arrangements that already pool risks. Its discussion explains that non-guaranteed lifetime-income arrangements can protect participants against individual longevity risk while adjusting benefits to available assets. It also describes examples introduced by employers or providers as payout options for particular employed populations. These are operating foundations for the proposal, although their existence does not establish the proposed combination across all intended populations.

In §5.1.2, the OECD explains that collectively defined ownership rights can support investment-risk sharing across cohorts and benefit smoothing, but may obscure how risks are distributed. The following discussion identifies individually defined rights as a way to make risk sharing more transparent. This is a design-specific trade-off, not evidence that all collective schemes have opaque transfers. In §5.1.4, the chapter explicitly connects benefit-adjustment rules to measuring financial imbalance and distributing mismatches among members.

The supplied review supports these historical findings through partially extracted source material. The retained HTML extraction ends during §5.4.2. The PDF extraction stops in Chapter 1 and includes pages without extractable text, so it does not independently fill the later chapter’s gaps. The PDF material reviewed does discuss pension-fund audits of financial statements, controls and accounting and actuarial assumptions, but completeness of the retained report cannot be certified from the supplied extraction.

Evidence scope: retrieval in November 2026 does not update findings published in 2022. The supplied search record is empty, leaving developments between that account and the review cutoff of 2026-11-01 unresolved. The inputs provide no verified quantitative comparison demonstrating the proposed improvement in costs, access or payment outcomes. These limitations prevent a current novelty or achievement claim; they do not show that the concept is infeasible or that subsequent results are false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: operate independently audited schemes across several populations, explicitly including participants with small balances. Specify the populations, observation periods, relevant existing-product comparators, benefit-adequacy measures and comparative cost and access thresholds before evaluating outcomes. Publish participation, exclusions, full costs and actual payment experience. These would be proposed evaluation criteria, not established industry standards.
completion_criteria.label: Audited schemes include small balances and publish actual payment experience

completion_criteria.text: Proposed disclosure and scrutiny: publish contractual ownership and adjustment rules, the method for measuring financial imbalance, who bears losses, and how members entering or leaving affect other participants. Report distributional effects across cohorts and participant groups. Independent review should examine the financial statements, controls and actuarial assumptions as well as whether actual adjustments followed the published rules. The OECD discussion grounds these subjects for scrutiny, but does not prescribe this complete demonstration program.
completion_criteria.label: Independent review checks actual adjustments against published risk-sharing rules

completion_criteria.text: Proposed resilience tests: combine observed experience with independently challenged stress tests covering specified adverse longevity, investment and funding conditions. Define stress severity in advance and report payment continuity separately from payment adequacy, including the size and duration of reductions. Identify any external financing or guarantees and their limits. A scheme should not receive credit for self-sufficiency when its demonstrated performance depends on additional resources.
completion_criteria.label: Stress-tested payment resilience accounts for reductions and external support

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and boundaries: disclose enough assumptions, methods and results for independent teams to reproduce the evaluation and test replication in additional settings. Report the conditions under which cost, access or payment targets fail. Finite operating histories and stress tests would establish demonstrated breadth under specified conditions, not universal reliability over every future lifetime. No such evaluation could establish adequate benefits under arbitrary adverse outcomes without adequate supporting resources.
completion_criteria.label: Evaluation disclosures enable independent reproduction and identify target failure conditions

related_concepts.text: ACT-03, A scalable actuarial architecture for financing correlated catastrophes, shares the broad problem of arranging risk pools and allocating shortfalls. The supplied research characterizes ACT-03 as arranging precommitted capital for correlated catastrophes, whereas ACT-07 concerns retirement income and individual longevity pooling. That distinction is consistent with the supplied titles, but ACT-03’s full record was not provided, so its detailed boundaries cannot be verified here.

Roster-based synthesis: ACT-04, Reliable long-horizon mortality and longevity forecasting with honest uncertainty, concerns a potentially important input to retirement-income design. Better forecasts could inform funding and benefit rules, while ACT-07 concerns how risks and resources are shared when outcomes differ from expectations. ACT-05, Dependable long-horizon economic scenarios for actuarial liabilities, similarly concerns financial scenarios that could inform evaluation; scenario quality alone does not supply assets or decide who bears losses.

Roster-based synthesis: ACT-01, Reliable actuarial measurement of unprecedented catastrophe losses, addresses catastrophe-loss measurement, and ACT-02, Trustworthy, near-instant insurance settlement at negligible per-claim cost, addresses claims settlement. Both connect broadly to dependable risk systems, but neither title describes the lifetime retirement-income allocation problem addressed here. ACT-06, Reliable long-term actuarial projection of healthcare costs under structural change, concerns another source of uncertainty relevant to retirement needs; forecasting those costs and pooling longevity risk remain distinct capabilities.

The supplied review also identifies overlap with lifetime annuities, collective defined contribution schemes, target benefit plans and tontines. These provide relevant precedents or comparison designs, rather than separate evidence that the proposed combined advance has been achieved. ACT-07 retains its identity as a demonstration goal spanning access, total cost, understandable rights and resilience; evaluating it requires comparison with existing arrangements on those dimensions.

brief.title: Affordable retirement income for life with clear rules
possible: People with modest retirement savings could turn them into payments that continue for life, through an affordable arrangement with clear rights. Members would share savings so that those who live longer keep receiving income after their own money would otherwise run out.
why: This could extend protection against outliving savings to retirees poorly served by existing pensions and insurance products. Clear rules would also help people understand whose payments or obligations change when the money falls short.

sources.showed: The OECD describes operating arrangements that share the risk of outliving savings. It explains how ownership rights and payment adjustment rules determine who bears financial shortfalls.
sources.cited_for: Existing lifetime payment arrangements provide foundations for combining shared risks with clear rights.
sources.not_established: Existing arrangements do not establish the full combination of broad access, low costs, clear rules and resilient payments across populations.

sources.who: Adam Butt, Gaurav Khemka and Eugene Tan
sources.showed: Their simulations studied pools where members can vary withdrawals. Limits on that flexibility kept the average loss in retirement income value below the extra charge on comparable guaranteed insurance payments.
sources.quote: However, with appropriate constraints on flexible payout structures, the average welfare loss is smaller than the loading applied to an equivalent annuity.
sources.cited_for: Withdrawal rules can limit the harm when members use knowledge of their health to choose payouts that benefit themselves.
sources.not_established: Simulations do not demonstrate actual costs, broad participation or lifetime payment outcomes in operating schemes.

sources.showed: Their mathematical analysis estimates how many members can receive stable lifetime income from a pool closed to new members. It holds investment returns constant and excludes the whole population living longer than expected.
sources.quote:
A numerical study suggests that the lower bound is close in value to the true
value.
sources.cited_for: Pool size affects how well individual differences in lifespan can be shared.
sources.not_established: This preprint does not establish payment stability under changing investment returns or unexpectedly longer lives across the population.

sources.showed: Their mathematical work examines when people of different ages and savings levels can share a pool with equal expected benefits per amount invested. Shares depend on age and investment size.
sources.cited_for: Sharing a pool across different groups requires explicit rules for distributing income rights.
sources.not_established: Mathematical conditions do not establish affordable administration, understandable contracts or successful operation across populations.

sources.who: Marcel Lever and Thomas Michielsen, CPB
sources.showed: Simulations found that sharing financial risks across generations could improve pension payments in bad economic conditions. The benefit depended on assumptions about investment returns.
sources.quote: The benefits of collective contracts are lower in simulations with a smaller equity premium.
sources.cited_for: Sharing financial losses can soften poor outcomes, but the gains depend on the financial assumptions.
sources.not_established: The model excludes uncertainty in lifespans and does not demonstrate actual lifetime payments or implementation costs.

shown: Employers and providers already offer arrangements that share savings to support lifetime payments. The OECD describes how payments can adjust to available assets. Mathematical studies and simulations explain parts of the design, including pool size, withdrawal flexibility and sharing losses across generations.
missing: A combined demonstration of broad access, low total costs, clear loss sharing and resilient lifetime payments, including for small savings.
Operating results showing how understandable, enforceable rules handle shortfalls and members joining or leaving.
Independent tests separating continued payments from enough income to meet needs, with any outside financial support made explicit.
Repeatable results across populations, with clear conditions under which cost, access or payment targets fail.

milestones.label: Audited schemes include small savings and report actual payments
milestones.explanation: Independently audited schemes would have to publish costs, access and actual payments across populations against comparisons and targets set beforehand. Including small savings would test whether access extends beyond wealthier retirees.

milestones.label: Actual adjustments follow published rules for sharing risks
milestones.explanation: Independent review would have to check finances, assumptions and actual adjustments against published ownership and loss rules, including joining and leaving. This would reveal who bears shortfalls and whether the rules hold.

milestones.label: Payments withstand defined stresses with reductions and support disclosed
milestones.explanation: Observed payments and independently challenged stress tests would have to report continuity, adequacy, cuts and outside support under adverse lifespan and financial outcomes. This would distinguish resilience from reliance on extra resources.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce results and identify failure conditions
milestones.explanation: Disclosed assumptions, methods and results would have to let independent teams reproduce evaluations and test other settings, including where targets fail. This would establish the demonstrated reach and limits of the design.

uncertain: The required improvements in cost, access and income adequacy still need defined thresholds.
Payments can continue for life yet fall below people's needs when investments disappoint or the whole population lives longer.
Results may depend on the population, local rules and financial support from employers or other organisations.

page.title: Retirement collective pension schemes
page.definition: In Great Britain’s proposal, a retirement collective pension scheme would be a section of a master trust or an unconnected multiple employer pension scheme. Members would acquire benefits through transferred pension rights or pension credit rights. Royal Mail’s whole-life collective pension also builds up benefits through payroll contributions. The retirement scheme would pool savings to pay income for life: money released when members die helps pay those who live longer. Payments could rise or fall with investment returns and with changes in how long the membership lives.

goal.need: In 2025/26, UK regulated firms reported 998,612 pension plans accessed for the first time. Savers took 45.6% of accessed pots entirely in cash. Someone drawing on an individual pot must decide how much to spend without knowing how long it must last. Pooling lets people who live longer keep receiving income without having to manage investments in old age. A guaranteed annuity also pays for life. Accepting variable payments leaves more scope to invest for growth, but pensions can fall if returns disappoint or members live longer than expected.

figures.caption: Estimated individuals aged 60–65 whose smallest non-zero defined contribution pension pot falls below alternative longevity-protection thresholds
figures.note: Consultation estimates from Figure 1, not observed exclusions. The proposed policy would assess combined relevant pension holdings within each provider.

statements.body: UK Department for Work and Pensions
statements.quote: By pooling longevity risk, RCPS (Retirement Collective Pension Schemes) can provide an income that is designed to last for life.
Retirement CDC schemes (R-CDC) could play a central role in meeting these objectives.
statements.context: The objectives are those of Guided Retirement, including access to a default way of drawing pension savings.

statements.quote: r-CDCs should be an option, but not framed as a solution for all
statements.context: The association warned that shorter life expectancy among poorer retirees could cause them to subsidise wealthier members.

completion.title: An authorised retirement collective pension scheme accepts its first transfer through Guided Retirement.
completion.criterion: Under the proposed framework, The Pensions Regulator authorises a retirement collective pension scheme and the scheme accepts its first transfer of a member’s pension savings through Guided Retirement. The proposed commencement period runs for 24 months from the regulator’s receipt of the application. The regulator may extend it by up to six weeks for good reason. Pension payments may start after the transfer.
completion.set_by: Department for Work and Pensions, retirement CDC policy consultation, paragraphs 20–22, and November 2026 draft regulations, regulations 8 and 18.
completion.threshold_quote: a person first accepts money as described in section 7(5)(a) of the Act.
completion.basis: The November 2026 proposals distinguish authorisation, acceptance of a transfer and payment of income. A member could enter through the designated default or actively choose the collective scheme from the defaults their provider offers. The proposed 0.75% annual charge cap applies to the collective fund.

milestones.title: Projected annual pension increases on the first ten years’ transfers match or exceed CPI inflation.
milestones.criterion: At application, identify the pension rights arising from expected transfers during the ten years from the scheme’s expected start. Project returns on the available assets over the remaining lives of the beneficiaries, including eligible survivors. On a central-estimate basis, the projected average annual increase in those benefits, applied over those remaining lives, must equal or exceed the projected average annual increase in the consumer prices index.
milestones.set_by: Department for Work and Pensions, draft regulation 8 inserting regulation 34A(3)(b), (5) and (6), the proposed first retirement collective money purchase scheme gateway test.
milestones.threshold_quote: is at least in line with the expected level of increase in the consumer price index (CPI)

milestones.title: A scheme secures resources for 24 months of run-on costs or justifies a shorter period.
milestones.criterion: The scheme has accessible resources for setup, ongoing operation, run-on costs and additional compliance costs following a triggering event, such as winding up. TPR assumes 24 months of run-on; a justified shorter period may be accepted, with six months the stated lower end. Legally enforceable third-party support may substitute for reserves. These resources cover administration and continuity, rather than guaranteeing benefit levels. DWP proposes extending the financial-sustainability requirements to RCPS.
milestones.set_by: The Pensions Regulator, CDC code, Financial resources, paragraphs 5–14. These requirements govern whole-life CDC schemes; DWP proposes their extension to retirement-only schemes in paragraphs 43–48 of its policy consultation.
milestones.threshold_quote: Schemes should assume a run-on period of 24 months.

milestones.title: An actuary certifies that a retirement collective pension scheme's design is sound.
milestones.criterion: The trustees obtain the scheme actuary’s viability certificate for their initial viability report. The actuary considers the first retirement gateway test and checks that the member booklet, statement of scheme design and quotation template accurately explain the benefit calculations, estimates and annual adjustments. For a scheme using cohorts, the actuary’s advice must also explain the rules for opening cohorts and why the mechanism preserves soundness.
milestones.set_by: The Pensions Regulator, Sound scheme design: introduction, paragraph 5, and DWP draft regulations 7, 8 and 11 on the retirement scheme’s viability report and certificate.
milestones.threshold_quote: the viability certificate provides the scheme actuary’s statement confirming that, in their opinion, the scheme design is sound.

milestones.title: The Pensions Regulator authorises a retirement collective pension scheme.
milestones.criterion: The Pensions Regulator grants authorisation to the retirement collective pension section after finding that it meets all applicable criteria under the proposed framework. These include sound design, financial sustainability, fit and proper persons, adequate member communications, effective systems and processes, and an adequate continuity strategy.
milestones.set_by: The Pensions Regulator, The authorisation criteria; extension to retirement-only schemes proposed by DWP in paragraphs 20–27 of its policy consultation.
milestones.threshold_quote: a CDC scheme meets all the authorisation criteria for it to be authorised and able to operate

milestones.title: A retirement pension model tests assets and benefits under adverse conditions.
milestones.criterion: Model the assets and pension liabilities of a retirement-only pool under a range of possible outcomes. Explain the assumptions and inputs, test sensitivity to alternative assumptions separately from market movements, and identify circumstances in which the design could cease to be sound, such as materially fewer entrants or significant pension cuts.
milestones.set_by: The Pensions Regulator, Viability report, paragraphs 7–10, for existing collective schemes. DWP proposes applying the viability-report framework to retirement-only schemes with modifications.
milestones.threshold_quote: stochastic asset liability modelling (ALM) alongside an explanation of assumptions and inputs

not_found: OECD, DWP, TPR and actuarial-body searches found no combined achievement benchmark for broad access, small-balance inclusion, total cost and lifetime payment adequacy.
No operational British retirement collective pension scheme or RCPS-specific authorisation was found in the government consultations or TPR's published register.
No prescribed minimum RCPS membership, inflow or pension balance was found; DWP's response explicitly leaves these scheme-specific.

results.finding: Common-adjustment tontine, 10,000 simulations of 1,000 members: adverse selection reduced the passive member’s payments by 0.17% per year on average in Case 4.
results.detail: Members in Case 4 are assumed to anticipate death and take the maximum payout in their final year. That leaves smaller balances to distribute as mortality credits.
results.quote:
Taking Case 4 as an example, the mean
MA
is 0.9983, indicating that on average the model member has a 0.17 per cent per annum reduction in payments due to the bias of pool member choice of
AIR
.

results.finding: Cohort-adjustment tontine, 10,000 simulations of 1,000 members: mortality-adjustment standard deviation reached 0.0538 at year 30.
results.detail: The appendix quantifies base-case volatility. It describes the corresponding adverse-selection results as similar to those for common adjustments and leaves their numerical results unpublished in the source.
results.quote:
For example, the standard deviation of
$M{A_5}$
is 0.0032, increasing to 0.0538 for
$M{A_{30}}$
, compared to a standard deviation of
MA
of 0.0074 at all ages using group-based adjustments.

results.finding: In a closed pool of 1,000 retirees, the modeled income stability bound extends through the 725th death.
results.detail: The example uses equal starting balances, the UK S1PFL life table and monthly payments. The 725th death is a conservative bound for the chosen tolerance and certainty.
results.quote:
However, for 90% of all samples, the income
stays between the income thresholds until 725 members died.

results.finding: In the closed tontine with one $100 investor, equity requires at least 23 members in the $1 cohort.
results.detail: Equity means equal expected lifetime payout per dollar invested. The supplied arXiv text identifies itself as an accepted manuscript and gives no journal publication details.

results.finding: In 5,000 equity-risk scenarios, the open whole-life CDC contract’s 5th-percentile annual change in real retirement payments was −3.3%.
results.detail: The open adjustment rule spreads funding shocks across years and future accruals. A cut can therefore be followed by further cuts. The simulations assume equal-sized cohorts and fixed lifespans.
results.quote: In the CDC open contract, the 5th percentile is -3.3% compared to -15.2% in the benchmark.

results.finding: Retirement-only CDC pool (999 base-case entrants per year): higher return volatility required a common one-off benefit adjustment in 39.6% of modelled years.
results.detail: The higher-volatility test holds mean returns fixed. When the long-term adjustment reaches the lower bound of CPI minus 2 percentage points, any remaining shortfall triggers a one-off cut that carries forward into future payments.
results.quote:
A one-third increase in the volatility of portfolio returns increases the 
rate of one-off adjustments from 33.1% to 39.6%.

results.finding: In 25,000 simulations, a 100-member open retirement pool with cohort-specific adjustments had a 42% expected probability of a cut of at least 5% at ages 90–105.
results.detail: The base case uses Canadian pensioner mortality with generational improvements and an equal stock–bond allocation. The report attributes the higher cut risk in the small open pool mainly to its mix of ages and the effect on how forfeited balances are shared.
results.quote: adjustments of 37% when the threshold is 0.95; it is 42% for the same open pool.

results.finding: For one illustrative retiree in a retirement-only CDC pool, longevity stress reduced the average income replacement ratio through age 90 to 30%.
results.detail: The longevity stress changes mortality improvements while keeping entry pricing fixed. The startup and poor-return scenarios show weaker benefits, but the report gives neither an entrant threshold for viability nor the size of any nominal pension cut.

On a central-estimate basis, the projected average annual increase in those benefits, applied over those remaining lives, must equal or exceed the projected average annual increase in the consumer prices index."; set_by = "Department for Work and Pensions, draft regulation 8 inserting regulation 34A(3)(b), (5) and (6), the proposed first retirement collective money purchase scheme gateway test."; set_by_kind = "government_programme"; threshold_quote = "is at least in line with the expected level of increase in the consumer price index (CPI)"; threshold_ref = 6; refs = [18, 5, 6]. Reason: The ten years define which transfers enter the calculation, while the projection covers beneficiaries’ remaining lives, and the closed-pool stability result measures a different outcome.

edit m2: title = "A scheme secures resources for 24 months of run-on costs or justifies a shorter period."; threshold_quote = "Schemes should assume a run-on period of 24 months."; threshold_ref = 8. Reason: The current title leaves the run-on period unspecified even though the regulator gives a 24-month starting assumption and allows a justified shorter period.
